name: Error Rate Problem
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: One Wrong Flip in a Thousand: The Error Rate Problem
lesson.summary: Explains gate and readout error rates in real quantum hardware, why errors compound multiplicatively across a circuit, and why this severely limits circuit size on today's devices.
lesson.body:
Qubit fragility, covered in the previous section, has a direct practical consequence: every operation performed on a real qubit, whether a single gate, a two qubit gate, or a final readout measurement, carries some probability of producing the wrong result. This stands in sharp contrast to classical computing, where individual logic gate operations are, for all practical purposes, considered error free, even though classical systems do use error correction schemes like ECC memory to guard against the exceedingly rare bit flip. The baseline reliability of a single classical transistor operation is astronomically higher than the baseline reliability of a single quantum gate today.

Giving a precise, universal number for current error rates is difficult because it depends heavily on the hardware platform, the specific type of gate, and the year, since the field is actively improving. As a rough sense of scale, leading platforms in recent years have reported two qubit gate error rates on the order of a fraction of a percent, meaning something like one error in every few hundred to roughly one thousand operations for the best demonstrated gates, with single qubit gates typically somewhat more reliable than two qubit gates. These figures continue to improve and vary enough between platforms and papers that they should be read as an illustrative order of magnitude rather than a fixed constant.

What makes even a seemingly small per-gate error rate a serious problem is that errors compound across a circuit. If each gate has an independent probability p of an error, and a circuit uses N gates in sequence, the probability that the entire computation completes without any error is roughly (1 minus p) raised to the power N. This shrinks quickly even for small p. As a concrete illustration, take p equal to 0.001, a rate in the ballpark described above, and N equal to 1,000 gates, a modest circuit by the standards of useful algorithms. Then (0.999) raised to the 1,000th power works out to approximately 0.37, meaning there is roughly a 63 percent chance that at least one error occurs somewhere in that circuit alone. Longer, more useful circuits make this worse quickly: a circuit with 10,000 such gates would have well under a 1 percent chance of running entirely error free.

This compounding is exactly why the theoretically promised algorithms described earlier in this book remain out of reach on today's hardware. Shor's algorithm applied to a cryptographically relevant number would require a circuit with a very large number of gates, far beyond what current error rates could tolerate without the output degrading into noise. The gap is not about whether the algorithm works in principle, that was settled by the theory, it is about whether physical hardware can execute enough gates reliably enough for the answer to mean anything.

The field's response to this problem is to distinguish between the physical error rate of the raw hardware and a much lower effective, or logical, error rate that can in principle be achieved by combining many physical qubits into error-protected logical qubits. That technique, quantum error correction, and the substantial resource cost it demands, is the subject of the final section of this chapter.
